newsitem.title: GERMANY: Major TV series planned on Germans and Holocaust.
newsitem.headline: Major TV series planned on Germans and Holocaust.

text.p: Germany's ZDF television plans a major documentary series on ordinary Germans and the Holocaust as a response to the charge by a U.S. academic that the whole Nazi-era population were "Hitler's Willing Executioners".

Guido Knopp, an award-winning ZDF documentary maker, said on Thursday evening the series would use hitherto untapped sources to show what average Germans knew and thought about the Third Reich's massacre of six million Jews.

A computerised evaluation of the vast records of the SS Security Service (SD) should provide the factual basis to rebut Harvard University professor Daniel Goldhagen's thesis that all Nazi-era Germans were obsessed with killing Jews, he said.

Goldhagen's book "Hitler's Willing Executioners" has caused an uproar this year in Germany, where most older people claim they knew little about Nazi crimes. Historians dismiss it as an emotional tirade but curious readers have made it a best-seller.

"Goldhagen asked the right questions but gave the wrong answers," Knopp said at a news conference to preview his latest series, "Hitler's Helpers", about top Nazi officials like Joseph Goebbels, Hermann Goering, Heinrich Himmler and Rudolf Hess.
"We have to give more solid answers."
Research for the next series, being carried out by a team of historians from Stuttgart and Jerusalem universities, would take about two years to complete, Knopp said.
By then, hundreds of thousands of secret weekly SD reports will be computerised and evaluated for the most complete picture ever compiled of public opinion in the Third Reich.
"This is one of the last great secrets of the Nazi era," said Knopp, whose last series -- a view of Hitler 50 years after the end of World War Two -- has been shown in 42 countries.

The popular TV historian said he had already thought about making a series based on the SD reports and was convinced this was needed after hosting public debates with Goldhagen during the author's book-promoting tour here in September.

The young American academic, son of a Holocaust survivor, claimed to know what the millions of Nazi-era Germans thought after looking into only a few thousand cases of policemen, concentration camp guards and anti-Semitic agitators.
"That is not serious history," Knopp argued. "I realised we are all groping around in the dark (about what Germans actually thought). He even said he didn't know."
The vast majority of SD reports have not been evaluated since the war. Only about five percent of them have been published to date, in a book called "Reports from the Reich".
"These are not propaganda reports," Knopp said. "They were for internal use only, from one functionary to another. They really wanted to know what people thought about this and that."

Post-war research shows Nazi-era Germans were not all rabid anti-Semites even though almost nobody dared to oppose the ruthless persecution of the Jews. Leading Nazis used to lament that Germans were not anti-Semitic enough.

"Based on a study of these sources, my feeling is that anti-Semitism was not the only and primary motive for the persecution of the Jews in the Nazi era," said Knopp, who was born in 1948. "There were many different reasons."
Knopp said the "Hitler's Helpers" series, which is due to be broadcast on ZDF in January and February, was three years in the making and thus not a response to Goldhagen's new book.
The public broadcaster's production will be a fuller version of the series of the same name which has just been broadcast on Arte, the French-German cultural channel.
Knopp, head of ZDF's contemporary history department since 1984, stressed it was important for German filmmakers to grapple with their dark past and present their findings to the world.
"We can't leave the world market to the BBC," he quipped.
